newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks rise on news of Kessler exit.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks rise on news of Kessler exit.

text.p: The stocks of tobacco companies ended broadly higher Monday on news that David Kessler, chief of the Food and Drug Administration and a vocal anti-smoking advocate, intends to leave his post.

Led by Kessler, who has been strongly critical of tobacco companies, the FDA has been considering a plan to regulate tobacco as a drug delivery device. Kessler will leave his post in early 1997 after a successor has been named, FDA officials said.

Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood, saw Kessler's departure as "a major plus ... for tobacco stocks. This vendetta they've had against the tobacco companies will probably lose some of its steam."

Philip Morris Cos. Inc., maker of Marlboro cigarettes, jumped $3.125 to $105.50, RJR Nabisco Holdings, which makes Camels, gained 62.5 cents to $32; Loews Corp., which owns Lorillard, was up $3.625 to $94.625, and UST Inc. added 87.5 cents to $32.75.
Analysts said, however, that a more important arena for the companies is the tobacco litigation is pending in courts around the country.
Emanuel Goldman at PaineWebber characterised the development as "the removal of a negative situation."
Whether tobacco companies are helped or hurt by Kessler's departure "depends on who takes over," Goldman added. "Certainly his leaving is not going to hurt tobacco companies."
Goldman noted that a Republican-controlled Congress or the courts could still block FDA efforts to regulate the industry.

Roy Burry, an analyst at Oppenheimer & Co., said that since the Clinton administration was behind the FDA's efforts, the departure of Kessler will have little effect because his successor will take the same stance.
"Any head of the FDA is going to be totally anti-tobacco and health-oriented," Burry said. "I don't think Kessler's leaving is going to have any effect."
Burry noted that a federal court in February will consider whether the FDA has jurisdiction to regulate the tobacco industry.

Proposed federal rules on tobacco seek to keep children from starting smoking by limiting their access to tobacco, reducing the appeal of advertising to youngsters and limiting the sale of child-oriented products such as caps or bags with tobacco company logos.
